The\n            caller then fits the periods one by one.\n\n        Notes\n        -----\n        The regressors of period ``bp`` are ``X = [F, D, ylag]``, where\n        ``F = [const, trend, lags]`` does not depend on the period, ``ylag``\n        is the lagged level and ``D`` holds the break dummies. Their rows\n        ``r >= s``, with ``s = bp - lags - 1`` (``bp - lags - 2`` for \"t\"),\n        form the tail, the others the head. Only the span of ``X`` matters\n        for the t-statistic of ``ylag``, so ``D`` is replaced by\n\n        * \"c\": the step ``1{r >= s}``,\n        * \"t\": the hinge ``(r - s + 1) 1{r >= s}``,\n        * \"ct\": both.\n\n        As ``F`` contains a constant and a trend, these are interchangeable\n        with their head versions ``1{r < s}`` and ``(s - 1 - r) 1{r < s}``,\n        which differ from the tail versions by a linear function of ``r``.\n        The shorter side is used, which keeps ``D`` far from ``F``.\n\n        Let ``A = [F, ylag, endog] = QR``. Then ``D = Qw + v`` with\n        ``w = Q'D`` and ``v`` orthogonal to ``A``. Row sums of ``Q`` over\n        the head (prefix sums) and the tail (suffix sums) give ``w`` of the\n        steps for all periods at once. The hinges follow from a second\n        cumulative sum, since ``(s - 1 - r) 1{r < s}`` is the sum of\n        ``1{r < j}`` over ``j < s``, and ``(r - s + 1) 1{r >= s}`` that of\n        ``1{r >= j}`` over ``j >= s``. ``D'D`` is known in closed form and\n        ``rho'rho = D'D - w'w`` gives the triangular ``rho`` with\n        ``v = V rho`` for an orthonormal ``V``. If -1 (default), uses ``n_blocks =\n        len(x)``, i.e., the classical delete-1 jackknife.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    JackknifeResult\n        A result object with fields:\n\n        theta_jack : float or ndarray\n            The bias-corrected jackknife point estimate.\n        se : float or ndarray\n            The jackknife standard error estimate.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    For data with serial dependence, ``n_blocks`` should be chosen small\n    enough (equivalently, block size large enough) that observations in\n    different blocks are approximately uncorrelated; this is a modeling\n    choice left to the user and is not verified automatically.\n\n    This implementation performs single-order bias correction only. A\n    known residual bias of order O(1/n^2) remains uncorrected; an iterated\n    jackknife (Schucany, Gray & Owen 1971) would address this at added\n    computational cost. Additionally, non-overlapping block placement\n    introduces some sensitivity to the arbitrary choice of block\n    boundaries; overlapping/moving-block schemes (Kunsch 1989) would\n    reduce this. Both are natural extensions but out of scope here.\n\n    To avoid O(n_blocks * n) cumulative memory allocation, a single\n    internal buffer is allocated once and reused across all delete-block\n    computations. As a result, ``statistic`` must not modify the array\n    it receives in place; doing so will silently corrupt results in\n    later iterations.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Quenouille, M.H. (1949). \"Approximate tests of correlation in\n       time-series.\" Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B,\n       11: 68-84.\n    .. [2] Tukey, J.W. (1958). \"Bias and confidence in not-quite large\n       samples.\" Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 29: 614.\n    .. [3] Kunsch, H.R. (1989). \"The jackknife and the bootstrap for\n       general stationary observations.\" Annals of Statistics, 17:\n       1217-1241.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    >>> import numpy as np\n    >>> x = np.random.normal(size=100)\n    >>> theta_jack, se = block_jackknife(x, np.mean, n_blocks=10)\n    \"\"\"\n    x = array_like(x, \"x\", ndim=1)\n    n = x.shape[0]\n\n    if n_blocks == -1:\n        n_blocks = n\n    n_blocks = int_like(n_blocks, \"n_blocks\")\n\n    if n_blocks <= 1:\n        raise ValueError(\"n_blocks must be greater than 1.\")\n    if n_blocks > n:\n        raise ValueError(\"n_blocks cannot exceed the number of observations.\")\n    if not callable(statistic):\n        raise ValueError(\"statistic must be callable.\")\n\n    block_sizes = np.full(n_blocks, n // n_blocks)\n    block_sizes[: n % n_blocks] += 1\n    block_bounds = np.cumsum(block_sizes)\n\n    theta_full = np.asarray(statistic(x))\n\n    max_reduced_len = n - block_sizes.min()\n    buffer = np.empty(max_reduced_len, dtype=float)\n\n    theta_delete = np.empty((n_blocks,) + theta_full.shape, dtype=float)\n    start = 0\n    for b in range(n_blocks):\n        end = block_bounds[b]\n        reduced_len = n - (end - start)\n\n        buffer[:start] = x[:start]\n        buffer[start:reduced_len] = x[end:]\n\n        theta_delete[b] = statistic(buffer[:reduced_len])\n        start = end\n\n    pseudo_values = n_blocks * theta_full - (n_blocks - 1) * theta_delete\n    theta_jack = np.mean(pseudo_values, axis=0)\n    variance = np.sum((pseudo_values - theta_jack) ** 2, axis=0) / (\n        n_blocks * (n_blocks - 1)\n    )\n    se = np.sqrt(variance)\n\n    if theta_full.shape == ():\n        theta_jack = float(theta_jack)\n        se = float(se)\n\n    return JackknifeResult(theta_jack, se)\n\n\nclass QStatResult(NamedTuple):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`q_stat`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    statistic : ndarray\n        Ljung-Box Q-statistic for autocorrelation parameters.\n    pvalue : ndarray\n        P-value of the Q statistic.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    statistic: np.ndarray\n    pvalue: np.ndarray\n\n\ndef q_stat(x, nobs):\n    \"\"\"\n    Compute Ljung-Box Q Statistic\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        Array of autocorrelation coefficients. Lags above m are left to ``yule_walker``.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    The autocovariances are computed exactly as ``yule_walker`` computes\n    them. The PACF at lag k is the last coefficient of the AR(k) Yule-Walker\n    solution, which is the k-th reflection coefficient of the Levinson-Durbin\n    recursion, so all lags are found in O(nlags ** 2) operations from a\n    single autocovariance sequence. The recursion stops at the first leading\n    Toeplitz matrix that is not positive definite, where it is no longer\n    known to be stable.\n    \"\"\"\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    pacf = np.empty(nlags + 1)\n    pacf[0] = 1.0\n    # Invalid values produce non-finite autocovariances, and yule_walker\n    # then repeats the calculation and its warnings\n    with np.errstate(all=\"ignore\"):\n        x = x - x.mean()\n        acov = np.empty(nlags + 1)\n        acov[0] = (x**2).sum() / nobs\n        for k in range(1, nlags + 1):\n            acov[k] = (x[:-k] * x[k:]).sum() / (nobs - k * adjusted)\n    if not np.all(np.isfinite(acov)):\n        return pacf[:1]\n    # phi[:k - 1] holds the coefficients of the AR(k - 1) model, and sigma\n    # its innovation variance\n    phi = np.empty(nlags)\n    sigma = acov[0]\n    for k in range(1, nlags + 1):\n        if not sigma > 0:\n            return pacf[:k]\n        refl = (acov[k] - phi[: k - 1] @ acov[k - 1 : 0 : -1]) / sigma\n        phi[: k - 1] -= refl * phi[: k - 1][::-1]\n        phi[k - 1] = refl\n        sigma *= 1.0 - refl * refl\n        pacf[k] = refl\n    return pacf\n\n\ndef pacf_yw(\n    x: ArrayLike1D,\n    nlags: int | None = None,\n    method: Literal[\"adjusted\", \"mle\"] = \"adjusted\",\n) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"\n    Partial autocorrelation estimated with Yule-Walker\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        The observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. All lags are computed from one autocovariance\n    sequence using the Levinson-Durbin recursion. ``yule_walker`` is used\n    for the lags where the recursion is not known to be stable, which are\n    those where the Toeplitz matrix of the autocovariances is not positive\n    definite.\n    \"\"\"\n    x = array_like(x, \"x\")\n    nlags = int_like(nlags, \"nlags\", optional=True)\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    if nlags is None:\n        nlags = max(min(int(10 * np.log10(nobs)), nobs - 1), 1)\n    method = string_like(method, \"method\", options=(\"adjusted\", \"mle\"))\n    if (x.ndim == 1 or x.shape[1:] == (1,)) and 0 < nlags < nobs:\n        pacf = _pacf_yw_levinson(x.reshape(-1), nlags, method == \"adjusted\")\n    else:\n        pacf = np.ones(1)\n    if pacf.shape[0] > nlags:\n        return pacf\n    with warnings.catch_warnings():\n        warnings.simplefilter(\"once\", ValueWarning)\n        rest = [\n            yule_walker(x, k, method=method, result_object=False)[0][-1]\n            for k in range(pacf.shape[0], nlags + 1)\n        ]\n    return np.concatenate([pacf, rest])\n\n\nclass PacfBurgResult(NamedTuple):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`pacf_burg`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    pacf : ndarray\n        Partial autocorrelations for lags 0, 1, ..., nlag.\n    sigma2 : ndarray\n        Residual variance estimates where the value in position m is the\n        residual variance in an AR model that includes m lags.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    pacf: np.ndarray\n    sigma2: np.ndarray\n\n\ndef pacf_burg(\n    x: ArrayLike1D, nlags: int | None = None, demean: bool = True\n) -> PacfBurgResult:\n    \"\"\"\n    Calculate Burg's partial autocorrelation estimator\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        Observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. Springer.\n    \"\"\"\n    x = array_like(x, \"x\")\n    if demean:\n        x = x - x.mean()\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    p = nlags if nlags is not None else min(int(10 * np.log10(nobs)), nobs - 1)\n    p = max(p, 1)\n    if p > nobs - 1:\n        raise ValueError(\"nlags must be smaller than nobs - 1\")\n    d = np.zeros(p + 1)\n    d[0] = 2 * x.dot(x)\n    pacf = np.zeros(p + 1)\n    u = x[::-1].copy()\n    v = x[::-1].copy()\n    d[1] = u[:-1].dot(u[:-1]) + v[1:].dot(v[1:])\n    pacf[1] = 2 / d[1] * v[1:].dot(u[:-1])\n    last_u = np.empty_like(u)\n    last_v = np.empty_like(v)\n    for i in range(1, p):\n        last_u[:] = u\n        last_v[:] = v\n        u[1:] = last_u[:-1] - pacf[i] * last_v[1:]\n        v[1:] = last_v[1:] - pacf[i] * last_u[:-1]\n        d[i + 1] = (1 - pacf[i] ** 2) * d[i] - v[i] ** 2 - u[-1] ** 2\n        pacf[i + 1] = 2 / d[i + 1] * v[i + 1 :].dot(u[i:-1])\n    sigma2 = (1 - pacf**2) * d / (2.0 * (nobs - np.arange(0, p + 1)))\n    pacf[0] = 1  # Insert the 0 lag partial autocorrel\n\n    return PacfBurgResult(pacf, sigma2)\n\n\ndef _pacf_ols_qr(x, nlags, efficient):\n    \"\"\"\n    Partial autocorrelations of the OLS estimator from a single QR\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : ndarray\n        The data series, 1d, demeaned by the caller. When efficient is\n        True, the regressions include a constant, so demeaning does not\n        change them but improves their conditioning.\n    nlags : int\n        The largest lag, at most nobs // 2.\n    efficient : bool\n        If True, the k-lag regression includes a constant and uses the\n        observations k, ..., nobs - 1. If False, it has no constant and\n        uses the observations nlags, ..., nobs - 1.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    ndarray or None\n        The partial autocorrelations for lags 0, 1, ..., nlags. None if a\n        regression is close to singular or the data are not finite, where\n        ``pacf_ols`` solves the regressions one by one.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    Gives the same result as the least squares fit of each regression in\n    ``pacf_ols``. The k-lag regression uses the first k columns of\n    ``[lag 1, ..., lag nlags]``, and a constant if efficient is True, so\n    ``nested_lag_ols`` gives the last coefficient of every regression. When\n    efficient is True the samples differ, and the regressions use the\n    observations k, ..., nobs - 1 through its ``start`` argument. The lags\n    before the start of the sample are set to zero, as in lagmat, and do\n    not affect the results.\n    \"\"\"\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    # lstsq treats singular values below max(nrows, ncols) * eps times the\n    # largest one as zero, and max(nrows, ncols) <= nobs\n    rcond = nobs * np.finfo(float).eps\n    if efficient:\n        # Row t of windows is x[t], x[t - 1], ..., x[t - nlags], with zeros\n        # before the start of the sample\n        padded = np.concatenate([np.zeros(nlags), x])\n        windows = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(padded, nlags + 1)\n        windows = windows[:, ::-1]\n        res = nested_lag_ols(\n            windows[:, 0],\n            windows[:, 1:],\n            np.ones((nobs, 1)),\n            rcond=rcond,\n            start=np.arange(nlags + 1),\n            check_fit=False,\n        )\n    else:\n        # Row t of windows is x[t + nlags], x[t + nlags - 1], ..., x[t]\n        windows = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(x, nlags + 1)[:, ::-1]\n        res = nested_lag_ols(\n            windows[:, 0], windows[:, 1:], rcond=rcond, check_fit=False\n        )\n    if res is None:\n        return None\n    pacf = res.params_last\n    pacf[0] = 1.0\n    return pacf\n\n\ndef pacf_ols(\n    x: ArrayLike1D,\n    nlags: int | None = None,\n    efficient: bool = True,\n    adjusted: bool = False,\n) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"\n    Calculate partial autocorrelations via OLS\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        Observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. If not, uses the same number of\n        observations to compute all pacf values.\n    adjusted : bool, optional\n        Adjust each partial autocorrelation by n / (n - lag).\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    ndarray\n        The partial autocorrelations, (maxlag,) array corresponding to lags\n        0, 1, ..., maxlag.\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n    statsmodels.tsa.stattools.pacf\n        Partial autocorrelation estimation.\n    statsmodels.tsa.stattools.pacf_yw\n         Partial autocorrelation estimation using Yule-Walker.\n    statsmodels.tsa.stattools.pacf_burg\n        Partial autocorrelation estimation using Burg's method.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    This estimates a separate OLS regression for each desired lag using\n    method in [1]_. The regressions share their regressors, so all of them\n    are computed from a single QR decomposition. Setting efficient to True\n    has two effects. First, it uses\n    `nobs - lag` observations of estimate each pacf.  Second, it re-estimates\n    the mean in each regression. j]\n            delta_b -= psi_prev[j] @ gamma[s - j].T\n\n        v_f = sig_f[0, 0]\n        v_b = sig_b[1, 1]\n        if not np.isfinite(v_f) or not np.isfinite(v_b):\n            pccf_vals[s - 1 :] = np.nan\n            break\n        tol = np.finfo(np.float64).eps * gamma[0].trace()\n        if v_f <= tol or v_b <= tol:\n            pccf_vals[s - The (1,2) element measures the partial association\n    from x to y, while pccf(y, x) measures the reverse direction.\n\n    The Yule-Walker methods use the multivariate Levinson-Durbin\n    recursion on the bivariate autocovariance matrix sequence. For\n    stationary series, this is asymptotically equivalent to OLS by\n    the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem [3]_, but is O(n * nlags)\n    versus O(n * nlags^3) for OLS. The two methods may differ\n    substantially on non-stationary (e.g., trending) data.\n\n    The \"ols\" method computes pccf(h) as the sample correlation\n    between the backward residual (x_t regressed on the\n    intervening observations) and the forward residual (y_{t+h}\n    regressed on the same intervening observations). Both\n    regressions include an intercept. For h=1, there are no\n    intervening observations, so pccf(1) is the correlation between\n    x[:-1] and y[1:].\n\n    For a bivariate VAR(p) process, P(h) = 0 for h > p,\n    providing a useful identification tool.\n\n    If the series are perfectly collinear or constant, the sample\n    autocovariance matrix is singular and the Yule-Walker methods\n    return NaN for all lags.\n\n    The OLS method returns NaN for lags where either residual series\n    has zero variance.\n\n    The confidence intervals use the asymptotic standard deviation\n    1/sqrt(n), following Wei (2006, Section 11.2) [1]_.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Wei, W. W. S. (2006). Time Series Analysis:\n       Univariate and Multivariate Methods, 2nd edition.\n       Pearson.\n    .. [2] Heyse, J. F. and Wei, W. W. S. (1985). Inverse\n       and partial lag autocorrelation for vector time series.\n       American Statistical Association Proceedings of Business\n       and Economic Statistics Section, pp. 233-237.\n    .. [3] Frisch, R. and Waugh, F. V. (1933). Partial time\n       regressions as compared with individual trends.\n       Econometrica, 1(4), 387-401.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    >>> import numpy as np\n    >>> from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import pccf\n    >>> rng = np.random.default_rng(12345)\n    >>> x = rng.standard_normal(100)\n    >>> y = 0.5 * x + rng.standard_normal(100)\n    >>> result = pccf(x, y, nlags=5)\n    >>> result_with_ci = pccf(x, y, nlags=5, alpha=0.05, result_object=True)\n    >>> result_with_ci.pccf.shape\n    (5,)\n    >>> result_with_ci.confint.shape\n    (5, 2)\n    \"\"\"\n    x = array_like(x, \"x\")\n    y = array_like(y, \"y\")\n    nlags = int_like(nlags, \"nlags\", optional=True)\n    methods = (\n        \"ols\",\n        \"yw\",\n        \"ywa\",\n        \"ywadjusted\",\n        \"yw_adjusted\",\n        \"ywm\",\n        \"ywmle\",\n        \"yw_mle\",\n    )\n    method = string_like(method, \"method\", options=methods)\n    alpha = float_like(alpha, \"alpha\", optional=True)\n    result_object = bool_like(result_object, \"result_object\", optional=True)\n\n    nobs = len(x)\n    if len(y) != nobs:\n        raise ValueError(\"x and y must have the same length\")\n    if np.any(~np.isfinite(x)) or np.any(~np.isfinite(y)):\n        raise MissingDataError(\"x and y must not contain NaN or inf values\")\n\n    if nlags is None:\n        nlags = min(int(10 * np.log10(nobs)), nobs // 2 - 1)\n        nlags = max(nlags, 1)\n    elif nlags <= 0:\n        raise ValueError(\"nlags must be a positive integer\")\n    if nlags > nobs // 2:\n        raise ValueError(\n            \"Can only compute partial correlations for lags up to 50% \"\n            f\"of the sample size. The requested nlags {nlags} must be \"\n            f\"<= {nobs // 2}.\"\n        )\n\n    if method == \"ols\":\n        ret = _pccf_ols(x, y, nlags)\n    else:\n        adjusted = method in (\"yw\", \"ywa\", \"ywadjusted\", \"yw_adjusted\")\n        ret = _pccf_yw(x, y, nlags, adjusted=adjusted)\n\n    confint = None\n    if alpha is not None and not 0 < alpha < 1:\n        raise ValueError(f\"alpha must be in the range (0, 1), got {alpha}\")\n\n    if alpha is not None:\n        interval = stats.norm.ppf(1.0 - alpha / 2.0) / np.sqrt(nobs)\n        confint = ret.reshape(-1, 1) + interval * np.array([-1, 1])\n\n    # PccfResult is always used when alpha is not None.  When alpha is\n    # None a bare array is returned, as before; pass result_object=True\n    # to always get a PccfResult.\n    if result_object or alpha is not None:\n        return PccfResult(ret, confint)\n    return ret\n\n\n# moved from sandbox.tsa.examples.try_ld_nitime, via nitime\n# TODO: check what to return, for testing and trying out returns everything\nclass LevinsonDurbinResult(NamedTuple):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`levinson_durbin`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    sigma_v : float\n        The estimate of the error variance.\n    arcoefs : ndarray\n        The estimate of the autoregressive coefficients for a model\n        including nlags.\n    pacf : ndarray\n        The partial autocorrelation function.\n    sigma : ndarray\n        The entire sigma array from intermediate result, last value is\n        sigma_v.\n    phi : ndarray\n        The entire phi array from intermediate result, last column\n        contains autoregressive coefficients for AR(nlags).\n    \"\"\"\n\n    sigma_v: float\n    arcoefs: np.ndarray\n    pacf: np.ndarray\n    sigma: np.ndarray\n    phi: np.ndarray\n\n\ndef levinson_durbin(s, nlags=10, isacov=False):\n    \"\"\"\n    Levinson-Durbin recursion for autoregressive processes\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    s : array_like\n        If isacov is False, then this is the time series. not tested\n\n    if order >= len(sxx_m):\n        raise ValueError(\n            \"The autocovariances available from s are too short for the \"\n            f\"requested number of lags: nlags={order} requires at least \"\n            f\"{order + 1} autocovariances, but only {len(sxx_m)} are \"\n            \"available.\"\n        )\n\n    phi = np.zeros((order + 1, order + 1), \"d\")\n    sig = np.zeros(order + 1)\n    # Analogous to a Goldfeld-Quandt test. The null hypothesis\n    is of no heteroskedasticity.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    resid : array_like\n        Residuals of a time series model.\n        The shape is 1d (nobs,) or 2d (nobs, nvars).\n    subset_length : int or float, optional\n        Length of the subsets to test (h in Notes below).\n        If a float in 0 < subset_length < 1, it is interpreted as fraction.\n        Default is 1/3.\n    alternative : {\"increasing\", \"decreasing\", \"two-sided\"}, optional\n        This specifies the alternative for the p-value calculation. That means different\n    things depending on which alternative is selected:\n\n    - Increasing: Null hypothesis is that the variance is not increasing\n        throughout the sample; that the sum-of-squares in the later\n        subsample is *not* greater than the sum-of-squares in the earlier\n        subsample.\n    - Decreasing: Null hypothesis is that the variance is not decreasing\n        throughout the sample; that the sum-of-squares in the earlier\n        subsample is *not* greater than the sum-of-squares in the later\n        subsample.\n    - Two-sided: Null hypothesis is that the variance is not changing\n        throughout the sample. Both that the sum-of-squares in the earlier\n        subsample is not greater than the sum-of-squares in the later\n        subsample *and* that the sum-of-squares in the later subsample is\n        not greater than the sum-of-squares in the earlier subsample.\n\n    For :math:`h = [T/3]`, the test statistic is:\n\n    .. math::\n\n        H(h) = \\sum_{t=T-h+1}^T  \\tilde v_t^2\n        \\Bigg / \\sum_{t=1}^{h} \\tilde v_t^2\n\n    This statistic can be tested against an :math:`F(h,h)` distribution.\n    Alternatively, :math:`h H(h)` is asymptotically distributed according\n    to :math:`\\chi_h^2`; this second test can be applied by passing\n    `use_f=False` as an argument.\n\n    See section 5.4 of [1]_ for the above formula and discussion, as well\n    as additional details.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. res2djoint.ssr)\n            / res2djoint.ssr\n            / mxlg\n            * res2djoint.df_resid\n        )\n        result[\"ssr_ftest\"] = (\n            fgc1,\n            stats.f.sf(fgc1, mxlg, res2djoint.df_resid),\n            res2djoint.df_resid,\n            mxlg,\n        )\n\n        # Granger Causality test using ssr (ch2 statistic)\n        fgc2 = res2down.nobs * (res2down.ssr - res2djoint.ssr) / res2djoint.ssr\n        result[\"ssr_chi2test\"] = (fgc2, stats.chi2.sf(fgc2, mxlg), mxlg)\n\n        # likelihood ratio test pvalue:\n        lr = -2 * (res2down.llf - res2djoint.llf)\n        result[\"lrtest\"] = (lr, stats.chi2.sf(lr, mxlg), mxlg)\n\n        # F test that all lag coefficients of exog are zero\n        rconstr = np.column_stack(\n            (np.zeros((mxlg, mxlg)), np.eye(mxlg, mxlg), np.zeros((mxlg, 1)))\n        )\n        ftres = res2djoint.f_test(rconstr)\n        result[\"params_ftest\"] = (\n            np.squeeze(ftres.fvalue)[()],\n            np.squeeze(ftres.pvalue)[()],\n            ftres.df_denom,\n            ftres.df_num,\n        )\n\n        resli[mxlg] = (result, [res2down, res2djoint, rconstr])\n\n    return resli\n\n\nclass CointResult(NamedTuple):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`coint`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    coint_t : float\n        The t-statistic of unit-root test on residuals.\n    pvalue : float\n        MacKinnon's approximate, asymptotic p-value based on MacKinnon\n        (1994).\n    critical_values : ndarray\n        Critical values for the test statistic at the 1 %, 5 %, and 10 %\n        levels based on regression curve. Starts with maxlag and drops a\n          lag until the t-statistic on the last lag length is significant\n          using a 5%-sized test.\n    return_results : bool, optional\n        For future compatibility, currently only tuple available.\n        If True, then a results instance is returned. 100 * SQRTEPS:\n        res_adf = adfuller(\n            res_co.resid,\n            maxlag=maxlag,\n            autolag=autolag,\n            regression=\"n\",\n            result_object=False,\n        )\n    else:\n        warnings.warn(\n            \"y0 and y1 are (almost) perfectly colinear.\"\n            \"Cointegration test is not reliable in this case.\",\n            CollinearityWarning,\n            stacklevel=2,\n        )\n        # Edge case where series are too similar\n        res_adf = (-np.inf,)\n\n    # no constant or trend, see egranger in Stata and MacKinnon\n    if trend == \"n\":\n        crit = [np.nan] * 3  # 2010 critical values not available\n    else:\n        crit = mackinnoncrit(N=k_vars, regression=trend, nobs=nobs - The other two fields are only\n    available through attribute access.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    statistic: float\n    pvalue: float\n    lags: int\n    harvey_adj_factor: float | None\n\n    _iter_fields: ClassVar[tuple[str, ...]] = (\"statistic\", \"pvalue\")\n\n\ndef diebold_mariano_test(\n    y,\n    forecast_a,\n    forecast_b,\n    *,\n    lags=None,\n    criterion=\"mse\",\n    power=2,\n    harvey_adj=False,\n    horizon=1,\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Performs a Diebold-Mariano test under the null hypothesis of\n    equal predictive accuracy between two forecasts.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    y : array_like\n        Array of the observed variable.\n    forecast_a : array_like\n        Array of forecasted values from the first model.\n    forecast_b : array_like\n        Array of forecasted values from the second model.\n    lags : int, optional\n        The number of lags to include in the Newey-West (HAC) variance\n        estimator used for the loss differential. Must be non-negative if\n        provided. If not provided, ``max(horizon - 1, ceil(nobs ** (1/3)))``\n        is used, so this also depends on ``horizon`` even when\n        ``harvey_adj`` is False. See the Notes for details.\n    criterion : str or callable, optional\n        The loss function used to score each forecast. Default is 'mse'.\n        Implemented criteria are 'mse', 'mad' (equivalently 'mae') and\n        'mape'; 'poly' selects a generalized power loss whose exponent is\n        set with ``power``. See the Notes for the definition of each\n        criterion. Alternatively, ``criterion`` can be a callable that\n        accepts two array_like arguments and returns an array of losses\n        with signature ``loss = criterion(y, forecast)``, allowing\n        problem-specific loss functions (e.g., QLIKE, see Examples).\n    power : float, optional\n        The exponent used to compute the loss when ``criterion='poly'``,\n        i.e., the loss is ``|y - forecast| ** power``. Default is 2, which\n        reproduces 'mse'. Ignored unless ``criterion='poly'``.\n    harvey_adj : bool, optional\n        Indicates if the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold (1997) correction for\n        small samples should be applied. Default is False. When True, the\n        test statistic is rescaled and the p-value is computed from a\n        Student's t distribution with ``nobs - 1`` degrees of freedom\n        instead of the standard normal.\n    horizon : int, optional\n        The forecast horizon used to (1) form the default number of HAC\n        lags and (2) compute the Harvey et al. (1997) adjustment when\n        ``harvey_adj`` is True. Must be a positive integer. Default is 1.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    DieboldMarianoResult\n        A result object containing the DM test statistic, its p-value, and\n        the Harvey et al. (1997) adjustment factor, if applicable.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    The Diebold-Mariano (1995) test compares the predictive accuracy of two\n    competing forecasts, ``forecast_a`` and ``forecast_b``, of the same\n    series ``y``. Accuracy is measured with a loss function :math:`g(y, f)`\n    (chosen via ``criterion``), and the test is based on the loss\n    differential\n\n    .. math::\n\n        d_t = g(y_t, \\\\text{forecast}_{a,t}) - g(y_t, \\\\text{forecast}_{b,t}).\n\n    Under the null hypothesis of equal predictive accuracy,\n    :math:`E[d_t] = 0`. The test statistic is the t-statistic from\n    regressing :math:`d_t` on a constant using a Newey-West (HAC)\n    covariance estimator with ``lags`` lags, i.e.\n\n    .. math::\n\n        DM = \\\\frac{\\\\bar{d}}{\\\\sqrt{\\\\widehat{\\\\mathrm{avar}}(\\\\bar{d})}},\n\n    where :math:`\\\\bar{d}` is the sample mean of :math:`d_t` and\n    :math:`\\\\widehat{\\\\mathrm{avar}}` is the HAC long-run variance\n    estimator. When ``lags`` is not supplied, a bandwidth of\n    ``max(horizon - 1, ceil(nobs ** (1/3)))`` is used. This differs from\n    some presentations of the DM test that always use ``horizon - 1``\n    lags; pass ``lags=horizon - 1`` explicitly to reproduce that\n    parameterization. Under the null, ``statistic`` is asymptotically\n    standard normal.\n\n    Because ``forecast_a`` and ``forecast_b`` are typically generated from\n    overlapping information sets (e.g., multi-step-ahead forecasts), the\n    loss differential is often serially correlated even under the null,\n    which is why a HAC estimator rather than the usual OLS standard error\n    is used.\n\n    For small samples, Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997) propose\n    rescaling the statistic by\n\n    .. math::\n\n        DM^{HLN} = \\\\sqrt{\\\\frac{T + 1 - 2h + h(h - 1) / T}{T}}\\\\, DM,\n\n    where :math:`T` is the number of observations and :math:`h` is the\n    forecast ``horizon``, and comparing ``DM^{HLN}`` to a Student's t\n    distribution with :math:`T - 1` degrees of freedom rather than the\n    standard normal. This correction is enabled with ``harvey_adj=True``.\n\n    The built-in criteria are:\n\n    * ``'mse'``: squared error loss, :math:`g(y, f) = (y - f)^2`. Penalizes\n      large errors more heavily than small ones; the corresponding DM test\n      answers \"which forecast has lower mean squared error?\"\n    * ``'mad'`` / ``'mae'``: mean absolute (deviation) error loss,\n      :math:`g(y, f) = |y - f|`. More robust to outliers than 'mse' since\n      errors are not squared.\n    * ``'mape'``: mean absolute percentage error loss,\n      :math:`g(y, f) = |(y - f) / y|`. Expresses errors relative to the\n      level of ``y``, which is useful when comparing series of different\n      scales, but is undefined when any element of ``y`` is zero and can\n      be dominated by observations where ``y`` is close to zero.\n    * ``'poly'``: generalized power loss, :math:`g(y, f) = |y - f|^p`\n      where :math:`p` is set with ``power``. Setting ``power=2`` is\n      equivalent to 'mse' and ``power=1`` is equivalent to 'mad'.\n\n    Any other loss can be supplied directly through ``criterion`` as a\n    callable, for example an asymmetric loss or a loss appropriate for\n    strictly positive series such as QLIKE (see Examples).\n\n    References\n    ----------\n\n    .. [1] Diebold, Francis X., and Roberto S. Mariano. \"Comparing predictive\n       accuracy.\" Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 13, no. 3\n       (1995): 253-263.\n    .. [2] Harvey, David, Stephen Leybourne, and Paul Newbold. \"Testing the\n       equality of prediction mean squared errors.\" International Journal\n       of Forecasting 13, no. 2 (1997): 281-291.\n\n    Examples\n    --------\n    Comparing two forecasts of a strictly positive series (e.g., realized\n    variance) using the QLIKE loss, which is standard in the volatility\n    forecasting literature and only defined for non-negative ``y`` and\n    strictly positive forecasts:\n\n    >>> import numpy as np\n    >>> from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import diebold_mariano_test\n    >>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)\n    >>> y = rng.standard_normal(200) ** 2\n    >>> scale = rng.chisquare(5, size=y.shape) / 5\n    >>> forecast_a = (0.9 * scale * y)\n    >>> forecast_b = scale * y\n\n    >>> def qlike(y, forecast):\n    ...     ratio = y / forecast\n    ...     return ratio - np.log(ratio) - 1\n\n    >>> res = diebold_mariano_test(y, forecast_a, forecast_b, criterion=qlike)\n    >>> res.statistic, res.pvalue  # doctest: +SKIP\n    \"\"\"\n\n    y = array_like(y, \"y\", ndim=1, maxdim=1, dtype=float)\n    forecast_a = array_like(forecast_a, \"forecast_a\", ndim=1, maxdim=1, dtype=float)\n    forecast_b = array_like(forecast_b, \"forecast_b\", ndim=1, maxdim=1, dtype=float)\n    lags = int_like(lags, \"lags\", optional=True)\n    harvey_adj = bool_like(harvey_adj, \"harvey_adj\")\n    power = float_like(power, \"power\", optional=True)\n    horizon = int_like(horizon, \"horizon\")\n\n    if horizon < 1:\n        raise ValueError(\"horizon must be a positive integer.\")\n    if lags is not None and lags < 0:\n        raise ValueError(\"lags must be a non-negative integer.\")\n\n    t = len(y)\n    if forecast_a.shape[0] != t or forecast_b.shape[0] != t:\n        raise ValueError(\"y, forecast_a and forecast_b must all have equal length.\")\n\n    if lags is None:\n        lags = int(max(horizon - 1, np.ceil(t ** (1 / 3))))\n\n    if isinstance(criterion, str):\n        criterion = string_like(\n            criterion, \"criterion\", options=(\"mse\", \"mad\", \"mae\", \"mape\", \"poly\")\n        )\n        if criterion == \"mse\":\n\n            def criterion_func(y, f):\n                return (y - f) ** 2\n\n        elif criterion == \"mape\":\n\n            def criterion_func(y, f):\n                return np.abs((y - f) / y)\n\n        elif criterion in (\"mae\", \"mad\"):\n\n            def criterion_func(y, f):\n                return np.abs(y - f)\n\n        else:  # criterion == \"poly\"\n\n            def criterion_func(y, f):\n                return np.abs(y - f) ** power\n\n    else:\n        criterion_func = criterion\n\n    # calculate d based on criterion\n    loss_1 = criterion_func(y, forecast_a)\n    loss_2 = criterion_func(y, forecast_b)\n    d = loss_1 - loss_2\n\n    # calculate test statistic as the t-stat of a constant-only HAC regression\n    res = OLS(d, np.ones_like(d)).fit(cov_type=\"HAC\", cov_kwds={\"maxlags\": lags})\n    dm_stat = float(res.tvalues[0])\n\n    # Harvey et. al (1997) small-sample adjustment\n    if harvey_adj:\n        adj_factor = np.sqrt(\n            (t + 1 - (1992)\n\n    This is the consistent estimator for the variance.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    resids : ndarray\n        The residuals from the regression used to compute the test.\n    nobs : int\n        The number of observations.\n    lags : int\n        The number of lags to use in the covariance estimate.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    float\n        The estimated variance.\n    \"\"\"\n    s_hat = np.sum(resids**2)\n    for i in range(1, lags + 1):\n        resids_prod = np.dot(resids[i:], resids[: nobs - i])\n        s_hat += 2 * resids_prod * (1.0 - (i / (lags + 1.0)))\n    return s_hat / nobs\n\n\ndef _kpss_autolag(resids, nobs):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes the number of lags for covariance matrix estimation in KPSS test\n\n    Uses method of Hobijn et al (1998). Assumes Bartlett / Newey-West kernel.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    resids : ndarray\n        The residuals from the regression used to compute the test.\n    nobs : int\n        The number of observations.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    int\n        The number of lags to use in covariance matrix estimation.\n    \"\"\"\n    covlags = int(np.power(nobs, 2.0 / 9.0))\n    s0 = np.sum(resids**2) / nobs\n    s1 = 0\n    for i in range(1, covlags + 1):\n        resids_prod = np.dot(resids[i:], resids[: nobs - i])\n        resids_prod /= nobs / 2.0\n        s0 += resids_prod\n        s1 += i * resids_prod\n    s_hat = s1 / s0\n    pwr = 1.0 / 3.0\n    gamma_hat = 1.1447 * np.power(s_hat * s_hat, pwr)\n    autolags = int(gamma_hat * np.power(nobs, pwr))\n    return autolags\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, repr=False)\nclass RURResult(LimitedIterationMixin[float]):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`range_unit_root_test` when ``result_object=True``.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    statistic : float\n        The RUR test statistic.\n    pvalue : float\n        The p-value of the test. Therefore, lags are\n    assumed to be in contiguous columns from low to high lag length with\n    the highest lag in the last column.\n    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: can tcol be replaced by maxlag + 2?\n    # TODO: This could be changed to laggedRHS and exog keyword arguments if\n    #    this will be more general.\n\n    method = string_like(method, \"method\", options=(\"aic\", \"bic\", \"t-stat\"))\n    results = {}\n    # Keep only the criterion of each fit unless the results are requested,\n    # since every results instance holds several nobs-sized arrays\n    crit = {}\n    for lag in range(startlag, startlag + maxlag + 1):\n        mod_instance = mod(endog, exog[:, :lag], *modargs)\n        res = mod_instance.fit()\n        if method == \"aic\":\n            crit[lag] = res.aic\n        elif method == \"bic\":\n            crit[lag] = res.bic\n        else:\n            crit[lag] = np.abs(res.tvalues[-1])\n        if regresults:\n            results[lag] = res\n\n    if method in (\"aic\", \"bic\"):\n        icbest, bestlag = min((v, k) for k, v in crit.items())\n    else:  # method == \"t-stat\"\n        # stop = stats.norm.ppf(.95)\n        stop = 1.6448536269514722\n        # Default values to ensure that always set\n        bestlag = startlag + maxlag\n        icbest = 0.0\n        for lag in range(startlag + maxlag, startlag - None\n        if the regressors are close to singular or the largest regression\n        fits almost perfectly. ``_autolag`` is used in these cases.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    Gives the same result as ``_autolag`` with OLS on the regressors\n    ``X = [trend, level, lag 1, ..., lag maxlag]`` that ``adfuller`` builds.\n    All candidate regressions use the first ``j`` columns of ``X`` and the\n    same sample, so ``nested_lag_ols`` gives the criteria of all lag\n    lengths from one QR decomposition without forming the lagged regressor\n    matrix.\n    \"\"\"\n    xdiff = np.diff(x)\n    nobs = xdiff.shape[0] - nobs2 * np.log(ssr / nobs) - nobs2\n        penalty = 2.0 if method == \"aic\" else np.log(nobs)\n        crit = -2 * llf + penalty * res.df_model\n        bestlag = np.argmin(crit)\n    return crit[bestlag], int(bestlag)\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, repr=False)\nclass ADFullerResult(LimitedIterationMixin[float]):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`adfuller`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    statistic : float\n        The test statistic.\n    pvalue : float\n        MacKinnon's approximate p-value based on MacKinnon (1994, 2010).\n    lags : int\n        The number of lags used.\n    nobs : int\n        The number of observations used for the ADF regression and\n        calculation of the critical values.\n    critical_values : dict[str, float]\n        Critical values for the test statistic at the 1 %, 5 %, and 10 %\n        levels. If -1 (default), uses ``n_blocks =\n        len(x)``, i.e., the classical delete-1 jackknife.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    JackknifeResult\n        A result object with fields:\n\n        theta_jack : float or ndarray\n            The bias-corrected jackknife point estimate.\n        se : float or ndarray\n            The jackknife standard error estimate.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    For data with serial dependence, ``n_blocks`` should be chosen small\n    enough (equivalently, block size large enough) that observations in\n    different blocks are approximately uncorrelated; this is a modeling\n    choice left to the user and is not verified automatically.\n\n    This implementation performs single-order bias correction only. A\n    known residual bias of order O(1/n^2) remains uncorrected; an iterated\n    jackknife (Schucany, Gray & Owen 1971) would address this at added\n    computational cost. Additionally, non-overlapping block placement\n    introduces some sensitivity to the arbitrary choice of block\n    boundaries; overlapping/moving-block schemes (Kunsch 1989) would\n    reduce this. Both are natural extensions but out of scope here.\n\n    To avoid O(n_blocks * n) cumulative memory allocation, a single\n    internal buffer is allocated once and reused across all delete-block\n    computations. As a result, ``statistic`` must not modify the array\n    it receives in place; doing so will silently corrupt results in\n    later iterations.\n\n    References\n    ----------\n    .. [1] Quenouille, M.H. (1949). \"Approximate tests of correlation in\n       time-series.\" Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B,\n       11: 68-84.\n    .. [2] Tukey, J.W. Lags above m are left to ``yule_walker``.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    The autocovariances are computed exactly as ``yule_walker`` computes\n    them. The PACF at lag k is the last coefficient of the AR(k) Yule-Walker\n    solution, which is the k-th reflection coefficient of the Levinson-Durbin\n    recursion, so all lags are found in O(nlags ** 2) operations from a\n    single autocovariance sequence. The recursion stops at the first leading\n    Toeplitz matrix that is not positive definite, where it is no longer\n    known to be stable.\n    \"\"\"\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    pacf = np.empty(nlags + 1)\n    pacf[0] = 1.0\n    # Invalid values produce non-finite autocovariances, and yule_walker\n    # then repeats the calculation and its warnings\n    with np.errstate(all=\"ignore\"):\n        x = x - x.mean()\n        acov = np.empty(nlags + 1)\n        acov[0] = (x**2).sum() / nobs\n        for k in range(1, nlags + 1):\n            acov[k] = (x[:-k] * x[k:]).sum() / (nobs - k * adjusted)\n    if not np.all(np.isfinite(acov)):\n        return pacf[:1]\n    # phi[:k - 1] holds the coefficients of the AR(k - 1) model, and sigma\n    # its innovation variance\n    phi = np.empty(nlags)\n    sigma = acov[0]\n    for k in range(1, nlags + 1):\n        if not sigma > 0:\n            return pacf[:k]\n        refl = (acov[k] - phi[: k - 1] @ acov[k - 1 : 0 : -1]) / sigma\n        phi[: k - 1] -= refl * phi[: k - 1][::-1]\n        phi[k - 1] = refl\n        sigma *= 1.0 - refl * refl\n        pacf[k] = refl\n    return pacf\n\n\ndef pacf_yw(\n    x: ArrayLike1D,\n    nlags: int | None = None,\n    method: Literal[\"adjusted\", \"mle\"] = \"adjusted\",\n) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"\n    Partial autocorrelation estimated with Yule-Walker\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        The observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. All lags are computed from one autocovariance\n    sequence using the Levinson-Durbin recursion. ``yule_walker`` is used\n    for the lags where the recursion is not known to be stable, which are\n    those where the Toeplitz matrix of the autocovariances is not positive\n    definite.\n    \"\"\"\n    x = array_like(x, \"x\")\n    nlags = int_like(nlags, \"nlags\", optional=True)\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    if nlags is None:\n        nlags = max(min(int(10 * np.log10(nobs)), nobs - 1), 1)\n    method = string_like(method, \"method\", options=(\"adjusted\", \"mle\"))\n    if (x.ndim == 1 or x.shape[1:] == (1,)) and 0 < nlags < nobs:\n        pacf = _pacf_yw_levinson(x.reshape(-1), nlags, method == \"adjusted\")\n    else:\n        pacf = np.ones(1)\n    if pacf.shape[0] > nlags:\n        return pacf\n    with warnings.catch_warnings():\n        warnings.simplefilter(\"once\", ValueWarning)\n        rest = [\n            yule_walker(x, k, method=method, result_object=False)[0][-1]\n            for k in range(pacf.shape[0], nlags + 1)\n        ]\n    return np.concatenate([pacf, rest])\n\n\nclass PacfBurgResult(NamedTuple):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`pacf_burg`.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    pacf : ndarray\n        Partial autocorrelations for lags 0, 1, ..., nlag.\n    sigma2 : ndarray\n        Residual variance estimates where the value in position m is the\n        residual variance in an AR model that includes m lags.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    pacf: np.ndarray\n    sigma2: np.ndarray\n\n\ndef pacf_burg(\n    x: ArrayLike1D, nlags: int | None = None, demean: bool = True\n) -> PacfBurgResult:\n    \"\"\"\n    Calculate Burg's partial autocorrelation estimator\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        Observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. When efficient is\n        True, the regressions include a constant, so demeaning does not\n        change them but improves their conditioning.\n    nlags : int\n        The largest lag, at most nobs // 2.\n    efficient : bool\n        If True, the k-lag regression includes a constant and uses the\n        observations k, ..., nobs - 1. If False, it has no constant and\n        uses the observations nlags, ..., nobs - 1.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    ndarray or None\n        The partial autocorrelations for lags 0, 1, ..., nlags. None if a\n        regression is close to singular or the data are not finite, where\n        ``pacf_ols`` solves the regressions one by one.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n    Gives the same result as the least squares fit of each regression in\n    ``pacf_ols``. The k-lag regression uses the first k columns of\n    ``[lag 1, ..., lag nlags]``, and a constant if efficient is True, so\n    ``nested_lag_ols`` gives the last coefficient of every regression. When\n    efficient is True the samples differ, and the regressions use the\n    observations k, ..., nobs - 1 through its ``start`` argument. The lags\n    before the start of the sample are set to zero, as in lagmat, and do\n    not affect the results.\n    \"\"\"\n    nobs = x.shape[0]\n    # lstsq treats singular values below max(nrows, ncols) * eps times the\n    # largest one as zero, and max(nrows, ncols) <= nobs\n    rcond = nobs * np.finfo(float).eps\n    if efficient:\n        # Row t of windows is x[t], x[t - 1], ..., x[t - nlags], with zeros\n        # before the start of the sample\n        padded = np.concatenate([np.zeros(nlags), x])\n        windows = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(padded, nlags + 1)\n        windows = windows[:, ::-1]\n        res = nested_lag_ols(\n            windows[:, 0],\n            windows[:, 1:],\n            np.ones((nobs, 1)),\n            rcond=rcond,\n            start=np.arange(nlags + 1),\n            check_fit=False,\n        )\n    else:\n        # Row t of windows is x[t + nlags], x[t + nlags - 1], ..., x[t]\n        windows = np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(x, nlags + 1)[:, ::-1]\n        res = nested_lag_ols(\n            windows[:, 0], windows[:, 1:], rcond=rcond, check_fit=False\n        )\n    if res is None:\n        return None\n    pacf = res.params_last\n    pacf[0] = 1.0\n    return pacf\n\n\ndef pacf_ols(\n    x: ArrayLike1D,\n    nlags: int | None = None,\n    efficient: bool = True,\n    adjusted: bool = False,\n) -> np.ndarray:\n    \"\"\"\n    Calculate partial autocorrelations via OLS\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    x : array_like\n        Observations of time series for which pacf is calculated.\n    nlags : int, optional\n        Number of lags to return autocorrelation for. x.mean()\n    yo = y - y.mean()\n\n    gamma = np.empty((nlags + 1, 2, 2))\n    for h in range(nlags + 1):\n        if h == 0:\n            gamma[h] = [[xo.dot(xo), yo.dot(xo)], [xo.dot(yo), yo.dot(yo)]]\n        else:\n            gamma[h] = [\n                [xo[h:].dot(xo[:-h]), yo[h:].dot(xo[:-h])],\n                [xo[h:].dot(yo[:-h]), yo[h:].dot(yo[:-h])],\n            ]\n        gamma[h] /= nobs - h if adjusted else nobs\n\n    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(gamma[0]) < 2:\n        return np.full(nlags, np.nan)\n\n    sig_f = gamma[0].copy()\n    sig_b = gamma[0].copy()\n\n    phi_prev = [None] * (nlags + 1)\n    psi_prev = [None] * (nlags + 1)\n\n    pccf_vals = np.empty(nlags)\n\n    for s in range(1, nlags + 1):\n        delta_f = gamma[s].copy()\n        delta_b = gamma[s].T.copy()\n        for j in range(1, s):\n            delta_f -= phi_prev[j] @ gamma[s - j]\n            delta_b -= psi_prev[j] @ gamma[s - j].T\n\n        v_f = sig_f[0, 0]\n        v_b = sig_b[1, 1]\n        if not np.isfinite(v_f) or not np.isfinite(v_b):\n            pccf_vals[s - 1 :] = np.nan\n            break\n        tol = np.finfo(np.float64).eps * gamma[0].trace()\n        if v_f <= tol or v_b <= tol:\n            pccf_vals[s - 1 :] = np.nan\n            break\n\n        d_f = np.sqrt(v_f)\n        d_b = np.sqrt(v_b)\n\n        pccf_vals[s - 1] = delta_f[0, 1] / (d_f * d_b)\n\n        try:\n            phi_ss = np.linalg.solve(sig_b.T, delta_f.T).T\n            psi_ss = np.linalg.solve(sig_f.T, delta_b.T).T\n        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:\n            pccf_vals[s - 1 :] = np.nan\n            break\n\n        phi_new = [None] * (nlags + 1)\n        psi_new = [None] * (nlags + 1)\n        phi_new[s] = phi_ss\n        psi_new[s] = psi_ss\n        for j in range(1, s):\n            phi_new[j] = phi_prev[j] - phi_ss @ psi_prev[s - j]\n            psi_new[j] = psi_prev[j] - psi_ss @ phi_prev[s - j]\n\n        sig_f = sig_f - phi_ss @ delta_b\n        sig_b = sig_b - psi_ss @ delta_f\n        phi_prev = phi_new\n        psi_prev = psi_new\n\n    return pccf_vals\n\n\ndef _pccf_ols(x, y, nlags):\n    \"\"\"PCCF via OLS regression on intervening observations.\"\"\"\n    nobs = len(x)\n    pccf_vals = []\n\n    for h in range(1, nlags + 1):\n        if h == 1:\n            resid_x = x[: nobs - 1]\n            resid_y = y[1:nobs]\n        else:\n            indices = np.arange(0, nobs - h)\n            n_carriers = 2 * (h - 1) + 1\n            if len(indices) <= n_carriers:\n                pccf_vals.append(np.nan)\n                continue\n\n            carriers = add_constant(\n                np.column_stack(\n                    [x[indices + j] for j in range(1, h)]\n                    + [y[indices + j] for j in range(1, h)]\n                )\n            )\n            targets = np.column_stack([x[indices], y[indices + h]])\n            coeffs = np.linalg.lstsq(carriers, targets, rcond=None)[0]\n            resids = targets - Must be non-negative if\n        provided. If not provided, ``max(horizon - 1, ceil(nobs ** (1/3)))``\n        is used, so this also depends on ``horizon`` even when\n        ``harvey_adj`` is False. See the Notes for details.\n    criterion : str or callable, optional\n        The loss function used to score each forecast. Default is 'mse'.\n        Implemented criteria are 'mse', 'mad' (equivalently 'mae') and\n        'mape'; 'poly' selects a generalized power loss whose exponent is\n        set with ``power``. See the Notes for the definition of each\n        criterion. Alternatively, ``criterion`` can be a callable that\n        accepts two array_like arguments and returns an array of losses\n        with signature ``loss = criterion(y, forecast)``, allowing\n        problem-specific loss functions (e.g., QLIKE, see Examples).\n    power : float, optional\n        The exponent used to compute the loss when ``criterion='poly'``,\n        i.e., the loss is ``|y - forecast| ** power``. Accuracy is measured with a loss function :math:`g(y, f)`\n    (chosen via ``criterion``), and the test is based on the loss\n    differential\n\n    .. math::\n\n        d_t = g(y_t, \\\\text{forecast}_{a,t}) - g(y_t, \\\\text{forecast}_{b,t}).\n\n    Under the null hypothesis of equal predictive accuracy,\n    :math:`E[d_t] = 0`. The test statistic is the t-statistic from\n    regressing :math:`d_t` on a constant using a Newey-West (HAC)\n    covariance estimator with ``lags`` lags, i.e.\n\n    .. math::\n\n        DM = \\\\frac{\\\\bar{d}}{\\\\sqrt{\\\\widehat{\\\\mathrm{avar}}(\\\\bar{d})}},\n\n    where :math:`\\\\bar{d}` is the sample mean of :math:`d_t` and\n    :math:`\\\\widehat{\\\\mathrm{avar}}` is the HAC long-run variance\n    estimator. When ``lags`` is not supplied, a bandwidth of\n    ``max(horizon - 1, ceil(nobs ** (1/3)))`` is used. This differs from\n    some presentations of the DM test that always use ``horizon - 1``\n    lags; pass ``lags=horizon - 1`` explicitly to reproduce that\n    parameterization. Under the null, ``statistic`` is asymptotically\n    standard normal.\n\n    Because ``forecast_a`` and ``forecast_b`` are typically generated from\n    overlapping information sets (e.g., multi-step-ahead forecasts), the\n    loss differential is often serially correlated even under the null,\n    which is why a HAC estimator rather than the usual OLS standard error\n    is used.\n\n    For small samples, Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997) propose\n    rescaling the statistic by\n\n    .. math::\n\n        DM^{HLN} = \\\\sqrt{\\\\frac{T + 1 - 2h + h(h - 1) / T}{T}}\\\\, DM,\n\n    where :math:`T` is the number of observations and :math:`h` is the\n    forecast ``horizon``, and comparing ``DM^{HLN}`` to a Student's t\n    distribution with :math:`T - 1` degrees of freedom rather than the\n    standard normal. This correction is enabled with ``harvey_adj=True``.\n\n    The built-in criteria are:\n\n    * ``'mse'``: squared error loss, :math:`g(y, f) = (y - f)^2`. Penalizes\n      large errors more heavily than small ones; the corresponding DM test\n      answers \"which forecast has lower mean squared error?\"\n    * ``'mad'`` / ``'mae'``: mean absolute (deviation) error loss,\n      :math:`g(y, f) = |y - f|`. More robust to outliers than 'mse' since\n      errors are not squared.\n    * ``'mape'``: mean absolute percentage error loss,\n      :math:`g(y, f) = |(y - f) / y|`. Expresses errors relative to the\n      level of ``y``, which is useful when comparing series of different\n      scales, but is undefined when any element of ``y`` is zero and can\n      be dominated by observations where ``y`` is close to zero.\n    * ``'poly'``: generalized power loss, :math:`g(y, f) = |y - f|^p`\n      where :math:`p` is set with ``power``. Setting ``power=2`` is\n      equivalent to 'mse' and ``power=1`` is equivalent to 'mad'.\n\n    Any other loss can be supplied directly through ``criterion`` as a\n    callable, for example an asymmetric loss or a loss appropriate for\n    strictly positive series such as QLIKE (see Examples).\n\n    References\n    ----------\n\n    .. (1992)\n\n    This is the consistent estimator for the variance.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    resids : ndarray\n        The residuals from the regression used to compute the test.\n    nobs : int\n        The number of observations.\n    lags : int\n        The number of lags to use in the covariance estimate.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    float\n        The estimated variance.\n    \"\"\"\n    s_hat = np.sum(resids**2)\n    for i in range(1, lags + 1):\n        resids_prod = np.dot(resids[i:], resids[: nobs - i])\n        s_hat += 2 * resids_prod * (1.0 - (i / (lags + 1.0)))\n    return s_hat / nobs\n\n\ndef _kpss_autolag(resids, nobs):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes the number of lags for covariance matrix estimation in KPSS test\n\n    Uses method of Hobijn et al (1998). See also Andrews (1991), Newey &\n    West (1994), and Schwert (1989). Assumes Bartlett / Newey-West kernel.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    resids : ndarray\n        The residuals from the regression used to compute the test.\n    nobs : int\n        The number of observations.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    int\n        The number of lags to use in covariance matrix estimation.\n    \"\"\"\n    covlags = int(np.power(nobs, 2.0 / 9.0))\n    s0 = np.sum(resids**2) / nobs\n    s1 = 0\n    for i in range(1, covlags + 1):\n        resids_prod = np.dot(resids[i:], resids[: nobs - i])\n        resids_prod /= nobs / 2.0\n        s0 += resids_prod\n        s1 += i * resids_prod\n    s_hat = s1 / s0\n    pwr = 1.0 / 3.0\n    gamma_hat = 1.1447 * np.power(s_hat * s_hat, pwr)\n    autolags = int(gamma_hat * np.power(nobs, pwr))\n    return autolags\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, repr=False)\nclass RURResult(LimitedIterationMixin[float]):\n    \"\"\"\n    Result of :func:`range_unit_root_test` when ``result_object=True``.\n\n    Parameters\n    ----------\n    statistic : float\n        The RUR test statistic.\n    pvalue : float\n        The p-value of the test. \"5%\": crit_value[1],\n            \"10%\": crit_value[2],\n        }\n        return pvalue, cvdict\n\n    def _quick_ols(self, endog, exog):\n        \"\"\"\n        Minimal implementation of LS estimator for internal use\n\n        Parameters\n        ----------\n        endog : ndarray\n            The dependent variable.\n        exog : ndarray\n            The independent variables.\n\n        Returns\n        -------\n        ndarray\n            The t-statistics of the estimated coefficients.\n        \"\"\"\n        xpxi = np.linalg.inv(exog.T.dot(exog))\n        xpy = exog.T.dot(endog)\n        nobs, k_exog = exog.shape\n        b = xpxi.dot(xpy)\n        e = endog - exog.dot(b)\n        sigma2 = e.T.dot(e) / (nobs - k_exog)\n        return b /     from the original (standardized) series under test.\n\n        Parameters\n        ----------\n        series : ndarray\n            The standardized series under test.\n        nobs : int\n            The number of observations in series.\n        const : float\n            The normalized constant term value to use in exog.\n        trend : ndarray\n            The normalized trend values to use in exog.\n        cols : int\n            The number of non-lag columns in exog.\n        lags : int\n            The number of lagged difference terms to include in exog.\n\n        Returns\n        -------\n        endog : ndarray\n            The standardized first difference of series.\n        exog : ndarray\n            The regressor matrix for the auxiliary regression.\n        \"\"\"\n        # first-diff y and standardize for numerical stability\n        endog = np.diff(series, axis=0)\n        endog /= np.sqrt(endog.T.dot(endog))\n        series = series / np.sqrt(series.T.dot(series))\n        # reserve exog space\n        exog = np.zeros((endog[lags:].shape[0], cols + lags))\n        exog[:, 0] = const\n        # lagged y and dy\n        exog[:, cols - 1] = series[lags : (nobs - 1)]\n        exog[:, cols:] = lagmat(endog, lags, trim=\"none\")[lags : exog.shape[0] + lags]\n        return endog, exog\n\n    def _update_regression_exog(\n        self, exog, regression, period, nobs, const, trend, cols, lags\n    ):\n        \"\"\"\n        Update the exog array for the next regression\n\n        Parameters\n        ----------\n        exog : ndarray\n            The regressor matrix to update in place.\n        regression : {\"c\", \"t\", \"ct\"}\n            The trend order to include in the regression.\n        period : int\n            The candidate break period.\n        nobs : int\n            The number of observations in series.\n        const : float\n            The normalized constant term value to use in exog.\n        trend : ndarray\n            The normalized trend values to use in exog.\n        cols : int\n            The number of non-lag columns in exog.\n        lags : int\n            The number of lagged difference terms included in exog.\n\n        Returns\n        -------\n        ndarray\n            The updated regressor matrix.\n        \"\"\"\n        cutoff = period - (lags + 1)\n        if regression != \"t\":\n            exog[:cutoff, 1] = 0\n            exog[cutoff:, 1] = const\n            exog[:, 2] = trend[(lags + 2) : (nobs + 1)]\n            if regression == \"ct\":\n lags\n    ):\n        \"\"\"\n        t-statistics of the lagged level for all candidate break periods\n\n        Parameters\n        ----------\n        endog : ndarray\n            The dependent variable of the auxiliary regressions.\n        exog : ndarray\n            The regressor matrix from ``_format_regression_data``.\n        regression : {\"c\", \"t\", \"ct\"}\n            The trend order to include in the regression.\n        periods : ndarray\n            The candidate break periods, increasing.\n        nobs : int\n            The number of observations in series.\n        const : float\n            The normalized constant term value to use in exog.\n        trend : ndarray\n            The normalized trend values to use in exog.\n        cols : int\n            The number of non-lag columns in exog.\n        lags : int\n            The number of lagged difference terms included in exog.\n\n        Returns\n        -------\n        ndarray or None\n            The t-statistic of the lagged level in the regression of each\n            period. None if there are no periods, the data are not finite, a\n            break dummy wraps around or has too few nonzero rows, or a\n            regression is (almost) singular or fits (almost) perfectly. The\n            caller then fits the periods one by one.\n\n        Notes\n        -----\n        The regressors of period ``bp`` are ``X = [F, D, ylag]``, where\n        ``F = [const, trend, lags]`` does not depend on the period, ``ylag``\n        is the lagged level and ``D`` holds the break dummies. Their rows\n        ``r >= s``, with ``s = bp - lags - 1`` (``bp - lags - 2`` for \"t\"),\n        form the tail, the others the head. Only the span of ``X`` matters\n        for the t-statistic of ``ylag``, so ``D`` is replaced by\n\n        * \"c\": the step ``1{r >= s}``,\n        * \"t\": the hinge ``(r - s + 1) 1{r >= s}``,\n        * \"ct\": both.\n\n        As ``F`` contains a constant and a trend, these are interchangeable\n        with their head versions ``1{r < s}`` and ``(s - 1 - r) 1{r < s}``,\n        which differ from the tail versions by a linear function of ``r``.\n        The shorter side is used, which keeps ``D`` far from ``F``.\n\n        Let ``A = [F, ylag, endog] = QR``. Then ``D = Qw + v`` with\n        ``w = Q'D`` and ``v`` orthogonal to ``A``. Row sums of ``Q`` over\n        the head (prefix sums) and the tail (suffix sums) give ``w`` of the\n        steps for all periods at once. The hinges follow from a second\n        cumulative sum, since ``(s - 1 - r) 1{r < s}`` is the sum of\n        ``1{r < j}`` over ``j < s``, and ``(r - s + 1) 1{r >= s}`` that of\n        ``1{r >= j}`` over ``j >= s``. ``D'D`` is known in closed form and\n        ``rho'rho = D'D - w'w`` gives the triangular ``rho`` with\n        ``v = V rho`` for an orthonormal ``V``. The subtraction cancels when\n        ``v`` is small relative to ``D``; for those periods ``w`` and ``rho``\n        are computed from ``D`` itself, orthogonalizing twice.\n\n        With ``[A, D] = [Q, V] [[R, w], [0, rho]]``, the triangular factor\n        of ``[F, D, ylag, endog]`` has ``R[:m, :m]`` (``m`` columns in\n        ``F``) in its leading block and the triangular factor of\n\n            T = [[w[m:], R[m:, m:]], [rho, 0]]\n\n        in its trailing block. With ``r_xx``, ``r_xy`` and ``r_yy`` the\n        entries of the latter for ``ylag`` and ``endog``, the coefficient of\n        ``ylag`` is ``r_xy / r_xx``, its standard error is\n        ``|r_yy| / sqrt(df_resid) / |r_xx|``, and so the t-statistic is\n        ``sign(r_xx) r_xy sqrt(df_resid) / |r_yy|``.\n        \"\"\"\n        nrows, k = exog.shape\n        if regression == \"c\":\n            dummy_cols, shift = [1], 0\n        elif regression == \"t\":\n            dummy_cols, shift = [2], 1\n        else:\n            dummy_cols, shift = [1, 3], 0\n        g = len(dummy_cols)\n        # First row of the tail of each period\n        starts = periods - (lags + 1) - shift\n        # A step needs one row on each side to differ from the constant, a\n        # hinge two to differ from the trend\n        min_rows = 2 if regression in (\"t\", \"ct\") else 1\n        if (\n            periods.shape[0] == 0\n            or nrows <= k\n            or starts[0] < min_rows\n            or nrows - starts[-1] < min_rows\n            or not np.all(np.isfinite(endog))\n            or not np.all(np.isfinite(exog))\n        ):\n            return None\n        eps = np.finfo(float).eps\n        # Relative size below which a singular value or residual is treated\n        # as rounding, with a margin of 10 over the cutoff of matrix_rank\n        rtol = 10 * max(nrows, k) * eps\n        # The first period is fitted by OLS, which raises if its regressors\n        # are not of full rank\n        exog = self._update_regression_exog(\n            exog.copy(), regression, periods[0], nobs, const, trend, cols, lags\n        )\n        sv = np.linalg.svd(np.linalg.qr(exog, mode=\"r\"), compute_uv=False)\n        if not sv[-1] > rtol * sv[0]:\n            return None\n\n        fixed = [i for i in range(cols - 1) if i not in dummy_cols]\n        fixed += list(range(cols, k))\n        m = len(fixed)\n        a = np.column_stack([exog[:, fixed], exog[:, cols - 1], endog])\n        q, r = np.linalg.qr(a)\n        p = q.shape[1]\n\n        # Use the head of a period if it is not longer than its tail\n        head = starts <= nrows - starts\n        step_len = np.where(head, starts, nrows - starts).astype(float)\n        hinge_len = np.where(head, starts - 1, nrows - starts).astype(float)\n        # prefix[j] is the sum of rows r < j of q, suffix[j] that of r >= j\n        prefix = np.zeros((nrows + 1, p))\n        np.cumsum(q, axis=0, out=prefix[1:])\n        suffix = np.zeros((nrows + 1, p))\n        suffix[:-1] = np.cumsum(q[::-1], axis=0)[::-1]\n        w_cols, norms = [], []\n        if regression != \"t\":\n            w_cols.append(np.where(head[:, None], prefix[starts], suffix[starts]))\n            norms.append(step_len)\n        if regression != \"c\":\n            hinge_prefix = np.zeros((nrows + 1, p))\n            np.cumsum(prefix[:-1], axis=0, out=hinge_prefix[1:])\n            hinge_suffix = np.cumsum(suffix[::-1], axis=0)[::-1]\n            w_cols.append(\n                np.where(head[:, None], hinge_prefix[starts], hinge_suffix[starts])\n            )\n            norms.append(hinge_len * (hinge_len + 1) * (2 * hinge_len + 1) / 6)\n        w = np.stack(w_cols, axis=-1)\n        dtd = np.empty((periods.shape[0], g, g))\n        for i in range(g):\n            dtd[:, i, i] = norms[i]\n        if g == 2:\n            # The hinge is zero where the step is, and sums to the off-diagonal\n            dtd[:, 0, 1] = dtd[:, 1, 0] = hinge_len * (hinge_len + 1) / 2\n\n        # Cholesky factor of v'v = D'D - w'w. A pivot that is a small fraction\n        # of the squared norm of its column has lost digits to cancellation.\n        gram = dtd - np.swapaxes(w, 1, 2) @ w\n        rho = np.zeros_like(gram)\n        accurate = np.ones(periods.shape[0], dtype=bool)\n        for i in range(g):\n            pivot = gram[:, i, i] - np.sum(rho[:, :i, i] ** 2, axis=1)\n            accurate &= pivot > 1e-3 * dtd[:, i, i]\n            rho[:, i, i] = np.sqrt(np.where(accurate, pivot, 1.0))\n            for j in range(i + 1, g):\n                off = gram[:, i, j] - np.sum(rho[:, :i, i] * rho[:, :i, j], axis=1)\n                rho[:, i, j] = off / rho[:, i, i]\n        rows = np.arange(nrows)\n        for idx in np.flatnonzero(~accurate):\n            s = starts[idx]\n            if head[idx]:\n                dummies = [rows < s, np.clip(s - 1 - rows, 0, None)]\n            else:\n                dummies = [rows >= s, np.clip(rows - s + 1, 0, None)]\n            if regression == \"c\":\n                dummies = dummies[:1]\n            elif regression == \"t\":\n                dummies = dummies[1:]\n            d = np.column_stack(dummies).astype(float)\n            w_d = q.T @ d\n            v = d - q @ w_d\n            w_v = q.T @ v\n            v -= q @ w_v\n            w[idx] = w_d + w_v\n            rho[idx] = np.linalg.qr(v, mode=\"r\")\n\n        t_mat = np.zeros((periods.shape[0], g + 2, g + 2))\n        t_mat[:, :2, :g] = w[:, m:]\n        t_mat[:, :2, g:] = r[m:, m:]\n        t_mat[:, 2:, :g] = rho\n        r_small = np.linalg.qr(t_mat, mode=\"r\")\n        diag = np.abs(np.diagonal(r_small, axis1=1, axis2=2))\n        col_norms = np.empty_like(diag)\n        col_norms[:, :g] = np.sqrt(np.diagonal(dtd, axis1=1, axis2=2))\n        col_norms[:, g:] = np.sqrt(np.sum(r[:, m:] ** 2, axis=0))\n        if not np.all(diag > rtol * col_norms):\n            return None\n        r_xx = r_small[:, g, g]\n        r_xy = r_small[:, g, g + 1]\n        return np.sign(r_xx) * r_xy * np.sqrt(nrows - k) / diag[:, g + 1]\n\n    def run(self, x, trim=0.15, maxlag=None, regression=\"c\", autolag=\"AIC\"):\n        \"\"\"\n        Zivot-Andrews structural-break unit-root test\n\n        The Zivot-Andrews test tests for a unit root in a univariate process\n        in the presence of serial correlation and a single structural break.\n\n        Parameters\n        ----------\n        x : array_like\n            The data series to test.\n        trim : float, optional\n            The percentage of series at begin/end to exclude from break-period\n            calculation in range [0, 0.333] (default=0.15).\n        maxlag : int, optional\n            The maximum lag which is included in test, default is\n            12*(nobs/100)^{1/4} (Schwert, 1989).\n        regression : {\"c\",\"t\",\"ct\"}, optional\n            Constant and trend order to include in regression.\n\n            * \"c\" : constant only (default).\n            * \"t\" : trend only.\n            * \"ct\" : constant and trend.\n        autolag : {\"AIC\", \"BIC\", \"t-stat\", None}, optional\n            The method to select the lag length when using automatic selection.\n\n            * if None, then maxlag lags are used,\n            * if \"AIC\" (default) or \"BIC\", then the number of lags is chosen\n              to minimize the corresponding information criterion,\n            * \"t-stat\" based choice of maxlag. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_011Ch8usjhZcsBrBsnYYBK6D","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"`zivot_andrews` is now much faster on long series. On the workload script it takes 0.004 s instead of 0.29 s, with the same lags (28), the same break index (752), and a statistic equal to about 5e-14 relative. The change is in `statsmodels/tsa/stattools/_stattools.py`: one new method, `_break_tvalues`, and a small helper, `_orthogonalize`. The existing tests in `test_stattools.py` and `test_lagselect.py` pass (523 passed, 1 skipped, 2 xfailed). I couldn't run `ruff`, because neither it nor flake8 is installed here.\n\n**Why it was slow:** the old code rebuilt and solved a full least-squares problem for every candidate break date, so the time grew roughly with the square of the series length times the square of the regressor count.\n\n**What the new path does:**\n- **One factorization:** most regressors (constant, trend, lagged differences, lagged level) don't depend on the break date. They and the dependent variable are factored once with a QR.\n- **Running sums for the dummies:** only the break dummies change between candidates. Since only the space they span matters, each is replaced by an equivalent simple step or kink, taken on whichever side of the break is shorter. Its fit against the factored regressors comes from running sums over the QR basis, for all candidates at once.\n- **Tiny solve per candidate:** what's left is a stacked QR of at most a 4×4 matrix per candidate, with no inverses or normal equations. The method's docstring writes out the algebra.\n- **Guard against lost digits:** where the shortcut would lose precision, that candidate is recomputed directly from its own dummy columns. On ordinary data this hardly ever triggers. I also forced it on for nearly every candidate as a check, and the results matched.\n\n**When it falls back:** the original loop runs unchanged when any of these hold:\n- there are no candidate dates;\n- there are no more rows than regressors;\n- a dummy would wrap around or have too few rows on either side (this covers `trim=0`, which the old code rejects with an error almost immediately);\n- the data aren't finite;\n- the first candidate's regressors aren't clearly full rank (so the existing \"not full rank\" error is raised exactly as before);\n- some candidate's fit is singular or perfect to working precision.\n\n**Timings in a fresh process, on one core:**\n\n| Series length | Old | New |\n|---|---|---|\n| 3,000 | 0.30 s | 0.004 s |\n| 6,000 | 1.6 s | — |\n| 30,000 | — | 0.03–0.06 s |\n| 100,000 (`trim=0.01`) | — | 0.12 s |\n| 200,000 (80 lags, `\"ct\"`) | — | 1.3 s |\n\nAt 200,000 most of the time is the single QR.\n\n**Results compared with the old code:**\n- **Ordinary series:** I compared all three `regression` options, all four `autolag` options, three `trim` values, explicit and default `maxlag`, lengths from 60 to 1,200 and several series types. The statistic and p-value agree to 1e-9 and the critical values, lags and break index are identical.\n- **One near-collinear type disagrees, and the new code is the accurate one:** a large level plus a strong trend with tiny noise differs from the old code by about 1e-7. Against a long-double reference fit of every candidate, the new code is within about 1e-12 and the old code is off by up to 1e-7. On two harsher inputs (a quadratic with 1e-6 noise, and a step with 1e-9 noise) the old code was off by up to 4e-2, and the new code stayed within 3e-8 of the reference.\n- **Difficult inputs:** NaN or inf values, constant or linear series, deterministic sinusoids, very short series, 2-D input, `trim` of 0 or above 1/3, and `maxlag=0` all give exactly the old results, exceptions and warnings."}],"container":null,"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"stop_details":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":2,"cache_creation_input_tokens":1230,"cache_read_input_tokens":113339,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":1230,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":0},"output_tokens":8,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"global","speed":"standard"},"diagnostics":null,"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"50aa7160-fa12-4714-985a-80d2a16b1b77","uuid":"80b654d9-44da-45ad-b421-bd924f45780c","timestamp":"2026-11-17T17:42:07.839Z"}
